chief_complaint: chronic disorganization, difficulty concentrating, task completion
hpi_details: A 26-year-old female presents for evaluation of lifelong disorganization, difficulty concentrating, and difficulty completing tasks, with similar symptoms present before age 12 and persistent impairment in adult responsibilities.
ideas: She thinks she was born naturally scatterbrained and lazy, or that modern digital screen addiction has ruined her ability to focus.
concerns: She is worried that missing deadlines and misplacing client documents will lead to a performance review and the loss of her job.
expectations: She hopes to undergo a cognitive evaluation to explain her focus troubles and leave with structured organizational strategies or medical treatments.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Adult ADHD is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Adult ADHD requires a persistent pattern of at least five inattentive and/or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, several before age 12, impairment in at least two settings, clear functional impact, and exclusion of alternative explanations; obtain collateral history or records when feasible.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic disorganization, difficulty concentrating, task completion

Key HPI features: A 26-year-old female presents for evaluation of lifelong disorganization, difficulty concentrating, and difficulty completing tasks, with similar symptoms present before age 12 and persistent impairment in adult responsibilities.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain vital signs, weight, cardiovascular and mental-status examination, and screen for suicide, self-harm, violence, psychosis, mania, intoxication/withdrawal, and inability to maintain safety. Record baseline blood pressure and pulse before stimulant treatment.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Adult ADHD.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.

Diagnosing ADHD from concentration complaints alone without verifying childhood onset, symptom count, cross-setting impairment, functional impact, and competing causes such as anxiety, depression, trauma, sleep disorder, substance use, or bipolar disorder.

Prescribing stimulants without assessing personal and family cardiovascular history, blood pressure/pulse, psychosis or mania risk, substance-use disorder, diversion risk, pregnancy considerations, contraindications, and interactions.
Missing acute suicide, self-harm, violence, psychosis, mania, intoxication/withdrawal, or severe self-neglect that needs urgent psychiatric or emergency assessment.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with a structured assessment and collateral history or childhood records where available; evaluate sleep, mood, anxiety, trauma, learning difficulties, and substance use before medication.

Use psychoeducation, organizational skills/CBT-based coaching, and accommodations as appropriate. Discuss stimulants and nonstimulants through shared decision-making only after baseline cardiovascular and psychiatric risk assessment.

Monitor blood pressure, pulse, weight/appetite, sleep, mood, psychosis/mania, misuse/diversion, adherence, and treatment response; arrange urgent assessment for acute safety risk or mental-status change.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 26-year-old woman with lifelong disorganization, poor concentration, and task-completion difficulty, reportedly present before age 12 with adult functional impairment. Establish symptom count, impairment in at least two settings, functional consequences, collateral history, sleep, mood, anxiety, trauma, substance use, and medication history.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, weight, cardiovascular and mental-status examination, and assess safety, psychosis, mania, and intoxication/withdrawal. Record baseline blood pressure and pulse and relevant personal/family cardiac history before considering a stimulant.
reference_soap.assessment: Possible adult ADHD; the available history supports childhood onset but is insufficient to confirm required symptom count and cross-setting impairment or exclude alternative causes.
reference_soap.plan: Complete a structured ADHD assessment with collateral/records where feasible and address sleep, mood, anxiety, trauma, learning, and substance contributors. Offer organizational/CBT-based supports and accommodations. If medication is appropriate, select stimulant or nonstimulant treatment through shared decision-making after cardiovascular, psychiatric, misuse/diversion, interaction, and pregnancy assessment; monitor vitals, appetite/weight, sleep, mood, psychosis/mania, and misuse. Escalate urgently for acute safety or mental-status concerns.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Adult ADHD
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Adult ADHD
Implement evidence-based management plan: Methylphenidate or Atomoxetine, lifestyle coaching

teaching.one_liner: Persistent neurodevelopmental pattern of inattentive and/or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms beginning before age 12, impairing at least two settings, and not better explained by another condition.

must_ask.say: Did you have similar difficulties with attention or focus before you were 12 years old?
Do these problems happen both at work and at home, or only in one setting?
Do you struggle with disorganization, losing things, or finishing tasks?
Have you ever used stimulants, cocaine, or other substances recreationally?
How is this affecting your job performance and relationships?
How is your sleep and mood? Have you had unusually high-energy periods, hallucinations, or thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?

must_ask.objective: Cardiovascular and diversion risk before stimulants
must_ask.say: Do you or close relatives have heart disease, fainting, sudden unexplained death, or high blood pressure, and has anyone asked you to share or sell medication?

history.answer: I've been having a really hard time staying organized, focusing at work, and actually finishing tasks on time.
It feels like it's been this way my whole life, but it has gotten much harder to manage over the past six months since my job responsibilities increased.
I lose my focus within minutes unless something is extremely exciting, and I constantly make careless mistakes or leave projects half-finished.
It happens every single day from the moment I wake up until bedtime.
It gets worse when I have to do boring paperwork or long independent projects; the only time I focus is right before a hard deadline when I panic.
I often feel physically restless, tap my feet, misplace my keys, and sometimes blurt out answers or interrupt people before they finish talking.
Even back in elementary school, my teachers wrote on report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreamed, had a messy desk, and forgot to turn in homework.
It affects me everywhere—at the office I miss deadlines, and at home my apartment is a complete mess and I forget to pay utility bills.
I was promoted to a project coordinator role six months ago, so having less direct supervision and way more independent scheduling really exposed how disorganized I am.
I have never seen a psychiatrist or been evaluated or treated for attention issues before.
I've bought planners, downloaded productivity apps, and set dozens of alarms, but I always abandon them after three or four days.
My manager gave me a warning last month about missed deadlines, and I feel overwhelmed trying to keep up with basic adult responsibilities.
history.topic: Impact on work and daily life

history.answer: My partner gets frustrated with me because I frequently forget things I promised to do and lose track of what they are saying mid-conversation.
My brain feels like it is constantly buzzing at night, so it takes me an hour or two to fall asleep, but once I sleep I get around six hours.
I feel discouraged and stressed about falling behind, but I don't feel depressed, worthless, or devoid of interest in hobbies.
I feel anxious when deadlines are looming, but I don't have constant worry about everything, panic attacks, or social fears.
I have never had periods of abnormally high energy where I stayed awake for days without feeling tired or spent reckless amounts of money.
No, I have never heard voices or seen things that others couldn't see, and I don't feel paranoid.
No, I have never had thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life, and I don't have any thoughts of harming anyone else.
I don't have any chest pain, heart palpitations, or shortness of breath, and no one in my family has ever had sudden unexplained heart problems.
I have never used illicit drugs, cannabis, or prescription stimulants, and I don't take anyone else's medications.
I am generally healthy and don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, asthma, or thyroid problems.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I just take an over-the-counter multivitamin every morning, nothing else.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic vapes.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two glasses of wine on a weekend dinner.
I work full-time as a marketing coordinator and share a rented apartment with a roommate.
My father was always very forgetful, messy, and constantly losing his wallet, but neither of my parents has an official psychiatric diagnosis.
My last period started about two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days.
My partner and I use condoms consistently every time, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.
I've spent my whole life thinking I was just fundamentally lazy and undisciplined, or that my phone and modern screen time completely ruined my attention span.

I'm so worried that my missed deadlines and messy paperwork will push my manager to put me on a performance improvement plan and fire me. I hope to get evaluated to understand why my brain can't stay focused and walk away with real strategies or treatment options to finally stay on track.
